title: Savoy College history — Fannin County Folk and Fact, 1977, Page 63
text:
[Masthead/advertisement clipping at top left:]
R. H. HALSELL,            LEWIS HOLLAND,
  Vice President.              President.

SAVOY COLLEGE

J. T. ASHCRAFT, }  Professors.
L. W. PIERCE,   }

This institution for the education of young men and young women is situated at Savoy in the western portion of the county, in the midst of a populous, peaceful and intelligent community. Thorough in all of its branches, the Savoy college stands in the front rank of Texas institutions of learning.

[Masthead/advertisement clipping at top right:]
MASONIC FEMALE INSTITUTE.
W. D. ALLEN,            President.
——BONHAM, TEXAS——

This college, for the education of females exclusively, was founded by the president in 1882. It is regularly chartered, having the power to confer degrees, and with its able faculty, is second to none in North Texas. The college building is ample, and handsomely appointed.

For particulars apply to, or address,
              Prof. W. D. ALLEN,
                        Bonham, Texas.

for the school but with the death of the great man whom an institution had been built around, it was practically impossible to maintain the forward progress of the founder. In 1913 the school joined with Carr-Burdette College in Sherman, but this effort was abandoned in 1916 and the graduates of Carlton College were adopted into the alumni fellowship of Texas Christian University.   BY BARBARA C. JONES

SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

Savoy Male and Female College was probably the first collegiate coeducational school in Texas to admit men and women to the same classes on the same academic standards. Founded in 1876 at Savoy, the college was chartered in 1880 by Robert R. Halsell, president, Lewis Holland, vice president and James L. German, Thomas Chenoweth and James Paxton, trustees. By 1885 the college was conferring B. S. and A. B. degrees. The A. B. degree required four years each of Latin, Greek and mathematics with courses in physiology, physics, chemistry, rhetoric and elocution. By 1887, 1888 enrollment was 66 with 102 and 133 pupils in the primary and preparatory departments. During the same years 44 Indian students, one of course came from across the Red River with federal funds for tuition.

Academic and social standards were strict with social contact between men and women students rigidly forbidden except on carefully chaperoned occasions. Extracurricular interests produced a dramatic club, debates and three literary societies, of which one published monthly "The Platonian Messenger", a combination literary magazine-newspaper.

The college building burned in 1890 and the school was not rebuilt until 1892. The founder is commemorated in the Halsell Memorial Gymnasium built for the Savoy public school through the Works Progress Administration funds in 1937. The Savoy Alumni Association, organized in 1937 with 128 members, has held annual reunions.

LADONIA MALE AND FEMALE INSTITUTE

Founded in 1860 by the Sister Grove Baptist Association comprised of 23 churches in seven counties, the Ladonia Male and Female Institute was organized in Ladonia instead of Bonham at the last minute because it offered a two-story building and more than $2,600 in donations. It then conducted a private school in the building and became the first principal with J. C. Averett becoming principal in 1861.

The school was moved in 1863 to a similar facility but soon closed because of inadequate enrollment. It was reopened by W. B. Featherstone in 1867 and returned to Ladonia in 1868. The school was finally closed in 1875 because of insufficient funding.

MASONIC FEMALE INSTITUTE

The Masonic Female Institute was the only institute or college in Fannin County devoted solely to the education of females. Operating during the late 1800's and located a half mile north of the courthouse in Bonham, the Institute was leased by the Constantine Lodge #13 to Professor E. H. Adams who was judged well qualified to educate, to discipline and to refine young women for the duties of home and society. S. D. Nunnelee, R. B. Scarborough, R. C. Thompson and J. A. Duncan were Masons serving on the committee which selected Adams. W. D. Allen presented J. A. Duncan as secretary; and J. W. Newman as treasurer. Primary courses included such subjects as reading, spelling, penmanship, primary arithmetic and geography. A preparatory course consisted of reading, spelling, penmanship, geography, English grammar and practical arithmetic. The collegiate course was divided into two departments: classical study and classical study. Collegiate departments cost $166 for boarding students and $41 for local students.

STEPHENSON SCHOOL

Among the many things connected with early history of Bonham is Stephenson school.

In the beginning it was organized as a private school and taught by Mrs. S. J. Stephenson in her home. The Stephensons had come to Bonham about 1884 from Lone Ridge, Arkansas and soon after their arrival Mr. Stephenson died leaving a widow and 6 children. About 1887 the widow erected a one room building on the front of her lot on south Main Street. The building is still standing at the south end of Main Street, having been remodeled and used as a residence. Inside the building the homemade desks seated two pupils, one large homemade blackboard was nailed across the east end of the building, which was heated by a woodburning stove in the center of the room. McGluffy's reader, Blue Back or Ray's arithmetic, Harvey's grammar and Rand McNally geography were the subjects taught.

About 1890 the school was incorporated into the public school system of Bonham and for awhile Vertus was the first superintendent. Classes from first through seventh grades were taught, but that soon changed as grades above third grade were transferred to a building called the college which was later named Duncan school. The older pupils who were transferred and later graduated with the 2nd graduating class of Bonham Public school in 1897 were Sophronia Bali, Clara Crittenden and Charlie Swope.
